work.title: History of Karka d-Beth Slok
work.edition: Machine translation (gpt-6.1-sol, Patristica, 2026-10-28) of: Paul Bedjan Acta martyrum et sanctorum 2; TEI by J. E. Walters, Digital Syriac Corpus (syriaccorpus.org 486)

paragraphs.text: The history of Karka d-Beth Slok (Kirkuk?) and its martyrs.

The foundations of this great city were laid by the king of Assyria who was nicknamed Sardanapalus. This king was great and feared throughout the whole world, and his kingdom comprised one-third of the inhabited world. This Sardanapalus was the son of Sennacherib, who was the thirty-second king in succession from Belus, the first king of the Assyrians. In the days of this Sardanapalus, Jonah was sent by God to Nineveh. Through his prophecy and preaching he stirred the Ninevites. Sardanapalus himself submitted to the prophet’s preaching and decreed a fast in Nineveh, and they put on sackcloth. God saw their repentance, as it is written, and turned his fierce anger away from them and did not destroy them. In the fifteenth year of that son of Nimrod, Arbaces, king of Media, against the kingdom of the Assyrians, to which he was subject. May the humble reader, the scribe, and the congregation that hears the history of the blessed man rejoice. May they be found worthy of mercy and compassion on the day of judgment and examination, through the grace of Christ, to whom belong glory and thanksgiving, and to his Father and to the Holy Spirit, praise, honor, exaltation, and dominion, now and always and forever and ever. Yes and amen. The history of the martyrdom of the blessed Mar Qardagh is finished. Glory to God. Amen.

was [?]; he openly rebelled. Now this Arbaces, when he rebelled against the kingdom of the Assyrians, gained power as time went on, grew stronger and more powerful, and became [?] toward the king of Assyria. When he had grown powerful, he began to attack the kingdoms that were subject to the king of Assyria, and took territories away from them. Afterward he came with an army to the region of Beth Garmai. At that time Garmay was a petty king, and he controlled the region. Arbaces carried off captives from him and plundered his domain. The kingdom of this Garmay, and the region over which he ruled, extended from the Zab River to the Tigris River, and from the Tigris to the mountain called Awrok, and from that mountain to the River Atherqon, which is also called Turmara, and as far as the region of Lareb and Mount Sha‘ran, and as far as the Little Zab itself. Garmay’s residence was at the fortress of Garmay, on that Mount Awrok, where his building is recognizable even now. When this Garmay was hard pressed by the kingdom of Arbaces and could not pay tribute to the kingdom of the Assyrians, he received from the kingdom of the Assyrians a governor over his kingdom and officials over his domain. And the assistance of [?] for those working on its wall. From that time Sargon ordered that, in that region,

under the authority of the kingdom of Beth Garmai, a city bearing his name should be built as a capital. In the territory of that authority, to which the whole region was subject as to [?], acting in the king’s place, it was built to be the capital of the dominion of that kingdom. Sargon built it, named the fortified city he had built after himself, and granted it freedom. He gave it the whole region in which it was established, so that its people would be its servants. He built a royal palace in the fortified city he had founded, and brought and settled there a great family from the land of the Assyrians, from among the kingdom’s nobles: a certain nobleman whose name was Burzen. He had built a small fortress for the city, situated it on the plain, and made a small wall for it. Along with that family and great lineage, he gathered about a thousand people from Assyria and settled them there, some inside the wall and some outside the wall. In the middle of the fortified city he built Sargon’s royal palace and the governor’s residence for the governor whom he had installed there. When the kingdom of Assyria began to come to an end, and Assyrian rule was being destroyed by divine judgment, Arbaces, who is Adorbad, built a strong defensive wall around the kingdom of the Medes. The region of Adorbaigan was named after him, and he began to advance against Nimrod with a great army. He met that Assyrian’s clan while he was encamped in Cilicia. They fought a battle, and the Assyrian was defeated

and killed in Cilicia. Afterward the kingdom of the Assyrians came to an end, and that of the Babylonians came to power. When this kingdom too was dissolved, that of the Medes arose. It too came to an end, and Darius son of Hystaspes reigned over Persia, the one whom the Magi call the son of Minats-hani: one of the kings who ruled Persia, who fought a battle with Alexander son of Philip and was defeated by him. He took Darius’s kingdom, and Alexander reigned over the kingdom of the Greeks. Because he had no sons, he divided his kingdom among four of his servants. After his death they took possession of his kingdom. One of them was named Seleucus. He built five fortified cities: Antioch, the city in Syria; Seleucia in Syria; Seleucia in Pisidia; Seleucia, the great city in the land of the Arameans; and the fortified city of Beth Selok. After Sardanapalus, Darius settled this fortified city and built a wall for it outside the wall that the king of Assyria had built. And he built houses there, and a fire temple alongside that temple of idols which Sardanapalus had established within it. The eagle and the earth were worshipped there. And Darius brought five families from the region of Istakhr and settled them within the city: their names are recorded in the archives of the Persian kingdom. After Darius came Seleucus, king of the Greeks, who is mentioned above.

He turned that wall of the city which had been built into a mound, and built a high wall above it. And he provided the wall he built with bastions—that is, sixty-five towers (towers?). He made one gate on its southeastern side, and another gate on its northwestern side. Above the southeastern gate he installed a full-length stone image of himself. To its right and left, beside this gate, were bastions of stone and mortar. This was the king’s gate. The other was called Tutai, after the man under whose supervision it had been built. Seleucus built a royal palace within the city, and laid out and embellished the city with streets and squares. He greatly enlarged it, not only within the wall but also outside the wall, and divided it into seventy-two streets. He brought five prominent families from Istakhr and settled them there, along with the other people whom he brought from various places. He gave these five families whom he had brought lands and vineyards in the region, and exempted the city from tribute. Twelve streets were named after twelve prominent families. The remaining streets were named after the trades. And Seleucus built, in memory of King Sardanapalus, who had first built the city: a colonnaded hall beside the royal palace which he had built within the citadel, which to this day is called Sarboi.

Thus the city remained pagan from the time it was built until the coming of the holy apostles: Addai and Mari, who were sent by the Holy Spirit to preach in our region. When they entered the city, they were welcomed by a man named Joseph. After he became a disciple and was baptized by them, he built the church which today is called the Monastery of Beth Joseph. From that time onward, the seed of faith in Christ sprouted in the city. Many of its people received baptism and became true Christians. And from the [?] of King Vologases until the twentieth year of Shapur son of Ardashir: For ninety years, Karka was a blessed field, and there were no weeds in it. But in the time of Shapur, Mani, the vessel of every evil, vomited his satanic gall (into it?). And it sprouted two weeds, whose names were Addai and Abzakhya, sons of the Evil One. Now in the time of Artabanus, king of the Arsacids, and during the reign of Hadrian Caesar, when persecution against the churches grew severe in the western region, the pastors and leaders there fled to the land of the East. A godly man named Theocritus had arrived in Karka as its head and leader. With the permission of the head who was in Shahrgard, this Theocritus became bishop in Karka, and he was ranked second to him, because metropolitan authority had been given by the apostles and by the see

of Antioch to Shahrgard. Theocritus was second, the bishop of Lashom third, the bishop of Hirbat-Glal fourth, and the bishop of Dara fifth. Theocritus himself built a church for the people of Karka, organized it, and established apostolic rules and ordinances in it, according to which the ministry of the clergy of Karka is conducted to this day. The church that Theocritus built is the one that John, the diligent pastor and pure priest, renovated there. After the death of Theocritus, Abdisho succeeded to his see, and bishops succeeded one another until the time of Mana, the bishop and victorious martyr. In his days, persecution arose against the Christians, and the church was demolished. Rebellion appeared even among the people of Karka themselves, and some of them were among those who demolished the church of their own city. Persecution took place in Karka not only through killing, but also through the plundering of property, imprisonment, and brutal flogging. So even women of the covenant, who had vowed virginity, who had come from the royal capital because of the persecution that had arisen against the church and were living in our city, were denounced before the commander of the infantry by some Manichaeans who were in the city. That accursed man ordered them to be killed outside the city, at a place called Hawra.

After these holy women received their crowns, at the place where they were crowned, a fig tree sprang up from their blood, and it brought healing to those who sought refuge in it. But when the Manichaeans saw the miracle that had occurred, they cut down the fig tree and burned the place where it stood. But God, who does not allow those who love him to be dishonored by their enemies, He afflicted them with dysentery, which ravaged them until they perished and disappeared entirely from the city. And that place, where the holy women won their victory, is called Beth Tetha to this day, and it has now become a refuge for all believers. Year after year, when they celebrate the commemoration of the great day of the Crucifixion, and the whole church assembly goes up to the great shrine of the martyrs, according to the city's custom, the shepherd and his flock in all its ranks, with the cross at their head and before them, turn aside to Beth Tetha in a great procession, with praises and holy songs of thanksgiving befitting God, the Lord of all, to the shame of unbelievers and the glory of believers. And upon us sinners may there be mercy, compassion, and salvation. Amen. Such were these events. But because of the severity of the persecution, a small number of people from Karka, together with the shepherd, a mighty warrior, at Hayarta beside Karka, in the woodland of a certain estate called Hasa, made small buildings to serve as a church. They used to receive Communion there secretly. When the misguided pagans learned about the steadfast

champion, they went there against him, and like vicious, merciless beasts they tormented him. When they saw that he would not submit to their wishes or exchange truth for falsehood, they stoned him on the ascent above Hasa. And he received the crown of martyrdom by being pelted with stones. After him, the blessed Isaac, from a well-known family, assumed leadership. He too was crowned with martyrdom. The nobles of Karka, who called themselves Christians in name, stoned him, having been compelled by the king's command. He was stoned on the hill above Kenar, the village in Neqator-Awna. After him John arose—the same John who, together with Mar Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, and John, bishop of Arbela, shone in the holy assembly of the three hundred and eighteen. After John, Aqballaha arose. This blessed man began the labors of virtue when he was about fifteen years old, and he used to give alms, so much so that he would secretly take gold, silver, and clothes from his parents and distribute them to strangers. When his father heard—he was at the royal court and held the position of tutor to Bazday— he denied Christ and worshiped fire in order to win the king's favor. But the blessed man left his parents' house and went away to live in a foreign land.

Because of his great labors and glorious achievements, he was chosen to take charge of his church in Karta. After taking office, he rebuilt the church that had been demolished in the days of Maʿna. He provided it with gold and silver ornaments, together with silk fabrics, vessels, and curtains, to equip it fully for worship. After his parents died, he gave the church all the treasure they had possessed. He made many people disciples and baptized them. Along with these, he also converted the village called Tishin— which was named after the ninety families whom King Shapur had brought from Maishan and settled there. They used to worship the demon Nani, whom they had brought with them from their homeland. One fifth of the village was the blessed man's ancestral inheritance— the property in Rawma that was called Khosrowan, after the blessed man's ancestors. The illustrious man made this village his disciple and brought it into the fold of life. Because of the signs and wonders that the heavenly command performed through his hands, news of his achievements spread swiftly and reached Bahram, son of Shapur, king of Persia, who had a daughter who was being tormented by an unclean demon. When Saint Aqebalaha was summoned there, he laid his hand on the girl, and she was healed. He persuaded the king that churches should not be demolished, and that those which had been demolished

should be rebuilt. The king listened to him, and his wishes were carried out. He uprooted and put an end to the two fools, Mani and Zoroaster, who appeared in the illustrious man's time, and to the unbelief and rebellion that had appeared among two families whom Sardanapalus had brought and settled in Karka. Their names were these: Parein, who denied the faith, and Balash, who rebelled. This evil inheritance in Karka belonged to Parein son of Amalca and to Balash. The illustrious Aqebalaha uprooted this evil seed and condemned them through his disputation. Nevertheless, sometimes openly and sometimes secretly, they persisted until the time of Khosrow, together with the bitter root of the accursed Mani; then they too came to an end. After Aqebalaha, God's holy man, fell asleep in death, the flock of the people of Karka chose Barhadbeshabba. For he was attested by signs and wonders and by every kind of virtuous deed. After this blessed man too had died, Xenaias succeeded him: a blameless and humble man, perfect in righteousness. And after this illustrious man too had departed to his Lord, his seat was occupied by Mar Shapur Braz of Karka, a chosen and virtuous man, adorned with spiritual beauty. His family was the one called the house of Ardashir son of Shapur Braz. This chosen man, however, relinquished his administrative office and went away to the monastery of the mourners. There he labored with them in chastity, in complete purity

and holiness. With the sword of the Spirit that he held, he uprooted and cleared away Mani’s weeds from the field of Karka. As for his kinsmen, who belonged to the families that Seleucus had brought from the region of Istakhr, he made them pure vessels for the Creator’s name. On their inherited property he built a house for strangers, where the sick, the distressed, the poor, and the needy are received and given rest. He endowed the house and set aside property for the wages of the physicians serving there and to supply the things needed by those who came for treatment. After he had been gathered in peace to his Lord, a victorious champion succeeded him, a chaste priest and a temple of holiness: Mar John, who attained perfection in both—that is, in priesthood and in martyrdom. In his time, Yazdegerd, who was the fifth after Shapur, was reigning in the land of Persia. Like Shapur, he too stirred up persecution against the Church of God, although for seven years he had ruled kindly. In the eighth year, he killed his daughter, who was his wife, and the nobles of his kingdom. He went to the region of Tashol and subjugated the petty kings there. There he built a city and named it after himself: Shahristan Yazdegerd. While he was there, he expelled the Christians from his army camp. The wretched man thought that his enemies were defeating him because of the Christians. He selected eight thousand Magian men and took away

their manhood, appointing them to serve him. Many of them died as a result of this decree. There was a custom among the kings of Persia that, at the beginning of each month, for seven days, each of the recognized officials would enter and present the case of those who had been wronged, and report to the king all affairs that were not being properly managed. That wicked man abolished this custom. When he returned from Tashol and came to his royal residence, he wrote to Tahmizgard, the Munrazdbed, who was in Nisibis: —which means administrator of the Magian religion—that Sarosha and the Razradi of the region of Arzon should go with him, whose name was Adofrazgard, together with the Dast Berham Rad of Adiabene and Beth Garmai, whose name was Surin. All three were to go to Karka and, through inducements and gifts, put pressure on the Christians of these four regions, which were governed by the four authorities mentioned above, until they denied Christ and worshiped fire. If they would not worship the sun or offer sacrifices to fire and water, they were to be handed over to flogging, torture with combs, and death by the sword. Tahmizgard and those with him arrived and entered Karka on the fifteenth of the month of Tammuz. They flogged the leaders, nobles, and other prominent people in Karka and threw them into prison. They sent merciless couriers

to distant regions and commanded them: “Bring here in harsh fetters every Christian you can find, so that, unless they renounce their faith, they may perish by various kinds of death.” When John, the bishop of Karka, saw what had happened, he wrote to the patriarch of Antioch, asking that they pray for him and his flock, that God would help them and bring them victoriously through this contest to which they had been called. Now holy John, from the day Tahmizgard entered Karka, from the fifteenth of Tammuz until the twentieth of the month of Ab, did not leave the sanctuary. Instead, he and his flock remained gathered in the church, calling upon God with groaning to come to their aid. During those very days, Tahmizgard gave orders, and they separated the shepherd from his flock and put him in prison, along with the many Christians imprisoned there. They were pressuring him to worship the sun. As he came out of the Lord’s house to go, he saw the judge and said aloud to Tahmizgard: “Peace to you, judge and one who will be judged! Peace to you, persecutor and one who will be tortured [?]! Peace to you, Magian, confessor, and martyr! Gather many for yourself, Tahmizgard! Gather a great company for yourself, with whom you will go to meet the bridegroom who has invited us to his kingdom. For look, I see

that you too, like Simon Peter, are destined to hang upside down on a cross for the name of Christ.” Imprisoned with blessed John were prominent men from the well-known family in Karka itself. Among them were Isaac son of Hormizgard, and Ardashir son of the man from Arzon, and Abraham, with seven others. Some of them remained steadfast in their faithfulness, while others renounced their faith. Now Isaac son of Hormizd, while he was in fetters because of his reverence for God, That blessed man opened his mouth and prophetically spoke to Tahmizgard words like those that the blessed John had spoken to him: “You, Tahmizgard, are destined to be crowned with noble martyrdom for our Lord. Instead of a wolf, you will become a lamb, and you will offer your body as a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.” Tahmizgard immediately gave orders, and the property and possessions of the pagan and Manichaean inhabitants of Karka were plundered. Those who had been ordered to gather Christians and bring them from every place went out with savage fury. They gathered and brought not only laymen and laywomen, but also bishops, priests, and deacons. These were the metropolitan of Arbela, the bishop of Beth Nuhadra, and the bishop of Maalta. With them were the metropolitan of Shahrgard, and second to him, John of Karka;

the third was the bishop of Lashom, the fourth of Mahoza, the fifth of Hirbat Glala, and the sixth of Dara, a village beside the Lesser Zab. These shepherds, together with their clergy and a great many of their flocks, came joyfully to Karka to receive the crowns of martyrdom with great gladness. As they entered, the cross, their boast, went before them, and they honored it in procession with a splendid service and songs of praise. Their number, according to the account, was one hundred and thirty-three thousand, besides the inhabitants of Karka who were confined in prison, who numbered twenty thousand. When those in prison heard the thunderous sound of the worship of those who had arrived, all the assembled people, invited to the kingdom, rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. But when Tahmizgard’s men saw the tens of thousands in the crowds and heard the loud sound of their praises, they were greatly alarmed, thinking that a rebellion had broken out. Tahmizgard went up to the place called Beth Tetta, where the martyrs had been killed in the days of King Shapur. He sat [?] on the judgment seat and arranged before those crowds all kinds of instruments of torture. He said to them, “King Yazdegerd has commanded as follows: If you do not obey his royal authority and his commands, and do not carry out his will, and do not worship the sun, the great god, and fire and water, the sons of Hormizd, you do not

honor, your lives will be destroyed by these instruments.” Along with the instruments of torture, they also had sixteen elephants, which they had brought to trample all those who would not deny Christ. But blessed Isaac took the instruments of torture and kissed them. He placed them over his eyes and said: “Peace to these irons, through which we enter that palace of the kingdom on high and delight in the dwellings of light prepared for us by our Lord Christ before the foundations of the world.” He opened his mouth and said to the judge, “Why are you standing there, judge? Come forward now and do what you have been ordered to do. For here we all are, ready to die joyfully for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” When the judge heard this, he gave orders, and they stretched Saint Isaac out on the ground by his four limbs. They drove nails into his hands and feet and scraped his body with iron combs until his flesh was stripped from his bones. While he was stretched out on the rock at Beth Tetta, and the wicked men were [?] him, his blood flowed down into the pit at Beth Tetta. While the saint was being tortured, Tahmizgard ordered that all those imprisoned for Christ should be brought to the courthouse beside Beth Tetta and questioned. If they did not renounce the name of Christ, they were to be tortured like Isaac. But the community

of holy and chosen Christians, knowing that the time when they would be crowned was near, gathered in the church, the shepherds together with their flocks. They celebrated the Eucharist and shared in the life-giving mysteries. They embraced and kissed one another with a holy kiss. Then they went out carrying a cross and proceeded to Beth Tetta, conducting the service as they went. When they saw Saint Isaac stretched out, with his body being scraped, they raised their voices and gave praise to God. They strengthened and encouraged the blessed man so that he would not lose heart amid these afflictions. Then the judge gave orders, and they brought naphtha, smeared the saint’s bones with it, and set them on fire. When the flames of the fire crackled among the champion’s bones, and he was close to departing to his Lord, he raised his voice and blessed the ranks of the Israel of God, and he was crowned with noble martyrdom. The judge ordered that after him they should bring the pure priest John, the bishop of Karkal. They brought him to the place where they had stretched out the champion Isaac, and cut off his hands. His blood flowed down into that pit at Beth Tetta. Then they brought him and sixty others who were with him to the valley east of Beth Tetta. Those saints, running swiftly and singing praise with the psalms of David, came to the place where death’s trap had been set. The judge gave orders, and they read the king’s decree before them.

There were ranks, gifts, and positions of authority in it for everyone who denied Christ. And for everyone who would not agree to deny him: the sword, fire, scourges, and scraping instruments. But the saints answered with one voice and said, “Let the king keep his gifts. Let him give positions of authority and ranks to others. We have a treasure in heaven that will never pass away. From there we await our life-giver, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to resemble his glorious body.” When the judge heard this, he gave orders concerning the champions. Some had their feet cut off; some had their tongues cut out; some had their eyes gouged out; and some had the skin stripped from their heads. To bring their struggle to its end, the judge gave orders, and they brought reeds and vine branches. They sought pitch to coat the wood, but they could find no pitch in our country. They coated it with naphtha and seated [?] the saints in the middle, with Bishop John at their head. They set fire to the wood and burned the bodies of the athletes. Thus they completed their martyrdom for Christ. Their number included the bishop, and Dadisho, Shubhalisho, and Bokhtisho, the priests who were with him, and twenty-eight well-known and faithful men from Karka itself. These received their crowns on the first day, on the twenty-fourth of the month of August, a Friday, in the sixth week after the Fast of the Apostles.

[?] On the twenty-fifth of that same August, a Saturday, they brought out to that place, where the first company had received their crowns, three thousand of the inhabitants of Karka, whose names are written in the Book of Life. Tahmizgard came out, and they built an altar [?]. They pressured the people of Karka to offer sacrifice. But those mighty in their God cried out and said, “Far be it from us to abandon Christ, who became a sacrifice for us, and offer sacrifice to rebellious demons!” When they subjected them to great afflictions, they grew all the stronger in Christ. As for the members of the clergy serving among them, whose names were Isaac [?] against them [?], they were stoned on the ascent above the village of Kenar. They crucified two women, daughters of the covenant from Karka itself, halfway up that ascent, and stoned them on their crosses. For Abraham, Simeon, and Ma‘na, they dug a pit at the top of the ascent, where Stephen and his companions had been stoned, and brought them there bound in heavy iron fetters. The rest of the blessed company of three thousand received their crowns at the place where John and his companions had been burned on the first day. As for Abraham, Simeon, and Ma‘ne and their companions mentioned above, they sent executioners [?] against them. They struck them with arrows in the very pit where they were sitting. They heated nails and drove them

into the pupils of their eyes, along with other nails, heated in the fire, with which they pierced the bodies of the victorious ones. These received their crowns on the second day, the twenty-fifth of August, a Saturday. On Sunday, the third day of the crowning of the victorious ones, Tahmazgerd gave orders, and they brought out to that place of judgment eight thousand nine hundred and forty people, whom they had brought from villages and cities far and near. With them were the metropolitan of Shahargard, the bishop of Lashom, those of Mahoza and Hirbat Galal, and the bishop of the village of Dara. When they had assembled, he seated the bishops separately, bound, and they brought that company of holy people in for questioning, group by group. When they had all confessed and had not denied their faith, and the pagans found that they all had one soul and one mind, the judge set against them about three thousand Magi, insolent and merciless men. Some of the holy people they slaughtered with the sword, and some they handed over to be burned in the fire. Others were sawn apart; others were stoned. Into the mouths, eyes, and nostrils of others they poured vinegar and bargantha, which is mustard, until they died. To put it briefly, through tortures and deaths

of various kinds they released the victorious ones from this world, so that they might pass to their homeland and go to their inheritance, which is light, life, and peace. Then one of the officials serving with Tahmazgerd was sent to the bishops mentioned above. He came and asked them, “Who is your head?” When they all remained silent, there was a young man imprisoned there, the son of a widow from Karka itself, whose name was Dindoy, like the earlier Dindon, who lived in the days of Shapur. It was because of this Dindon that metropolitan status came to Karka. He stood up courageously and said to the fathers, “Our fathers, be strong in our Lord and do not be afraid. Give an answer to the enemies. Otherwise, give your consent to the primacy of Karka, and we will endure the persecutors’ tortures in your place.” Then, at that very hour, the metropolitan of Shahargard and the bishops with him agreed, put it in writing, and affixed their seals to the document, saying, “Metropolitan status rightfully belongs to you, young man. who became a second Elijah and a young David at this hour of distress. From that day onward, the authority of the metropolitan see was firmly established in Karka. They laid their hands on him and blessed him while they themselves were in chains. When the pagans saw that the Christians stood firm in what they gloried in, and followed their rules without fear, they slaughtered them with swords. First they killed

the glorious Dindon, and then the bishops and the others with them, some from Karka and some from various other places. Now a woman from the neighborhood of Beth Zadok, whose name was Shirin, was baking bread in her house. When she heard that the saints had been crowned, she hurriedly left her bread and her dough and took her two sons with her, one on her shoulder and one by the hand. She ran and found the judge Tahmizgard below the poplar tree. Taking hold of the bridle of the horse he was riding, she implored him in Persian not to deprive her of the path along which the holy martyrs had been sent. The judge turned around, astonished at the matter. After he had urged the woman to abandon the resolve in which she stood firm, and she would not be persuaded, he gave an order concerning her, and her head was cut off with a sword, as was that of her older son. Her younger son fell weeping upon the bodies of his mother and brother and took some of their blood and rubbed it on his eyes and his body. Whenever the judge and the pagans took him over to themselves and tried to coax him with gifts and words, he would run back to the bodies of his mother and brother. He would fall upon them and kiss them, weeping. Then the accursed men killed him too. After these people had been killed, the Lord opened Tahmizgard’s eyes, and he saw a ladder set on the earth, with its top reaching

to heaven, and all those he had killed were climbing it. The Lord stood above it and placed splendid, glorious crowns on them. Immediately the judge’s mind turned to repentance, and he cried out in a loud voice, “I am a Christian,” in accordance with the prophecies about him. He lamented over himself and wept, pleading with Christ to forgive him for the blood of the martyrs that he had shed. When King Yazdegerd heard that Tahmizgard had abandoned the Magian religion and confessed Christ, he ordered that he be interrogated under the lash. After they had subjected him to tortures, chains, imprisonment, blows, and scraping combs, When they saw that he had not faltered in the struggle, the king ordered that he be hung upside down on a cross. Thus the blessed Tahmazgerd was crowned with noble martyrdom on the twenty-fifth of the month of September, a Monday. At the time of his crowning, he prayed and asked God that everyone who remembered the name of Tahmazgerd, in any affliction or illness whatsoever, might receive help from God. This, then, was the manner in which these twelve thousand martyrs were crowned, and thus they were brought to fulfillment with crowns of victory. Through their prayers, may our Lord make us all worthy of their sure hope and their glorious delight. Now the blessed Maron, the bishop of Karka itself, because of the love of God that was in him, built, at the place where they had been crowned—

the victorious martyrs—a monastery. Every year he held a commemoration for them with the burning fervor of his faith. Together with Mar Babowai the catholicos, he assembled a synod of the bishops of Beth Garmai and also of Adiabene. They wrote, sealed, and established by a binding agreement that a commemorative feast for these saints should be held for three days each year: namely, on the Friday, Saturday, and Sunday of the sixth week after the Fast of the Apostles. For the metropolitan of Adiabene had also been crowned there, as had the bishop of Beth Nuhadra, the bishop of Maalta, and the others with them, who had been crowned as victors in that great company. And it stands written and deposited in the archives of the church of the metropolitan city that any bishop from the dioceses of Karka who neglects to come to the assembly honoring the victorious martyrs, except because of illness or some unavoidable circumstance, and who deliberately disregards and despises the canon established by the fathers, is not permitted, by the word of our Lord, to carry out his ministry. Such is the wondrous victory of the saints and the labor of their glorious struggle, these radiant martyrs and resolute athletes. It has been told very briefly, and I thought these things sufficient, even though lovers of learning long to hear more. But we, [?], heirs and children of the saints, and heirs of Christ who crowns them,

let us take refuge in their prayers and implore their Lord, the Lord of all, that his peace, tranquility, and mercy may overflow to all the ends of creation; and that in his compassion he may preserve his church, in the splendor of the saints within it, until his appearing from heaven; and that he may adorn it with the well-being of its pure and diligent shepherds, according to his promise to it. And for the holy mountain, the second Sinai, the dwelling place of the divine presence, the tabernacle of light where [?] the treasure of the saints’ bones: may praise increase within it, and may thanksgiving grow within it. And may her horn be raised to heaven through the power of the victorious ones, the holy stones laid in his courts. And may he make glorious the diligent workers who serve the Lord within her and please him, so that divine grace may show them to be servants of righteousness and holiness, like beloved children of the victorious martyrs. And for the man of God, outstanding in the Lord’s work, the steward of his holy house, distinguished in good deeds, who serves in his fathers’ house with exemplary conduct, may the Lord increase through his hands the bounty of his right hand, with every increase of blessings from heaven and earth, through the prayers of the saints; and may he be found worthy of the light in their dwellings. May our Lord Jesus Christ, God over all, also make worthy of that light and that glory our congregation in all its ranks and orders. Amen. We also make this known: that our fathers ordained this from

ancient times: that on Friday there should be a commemoration of the victorious martyrs, of the metropolitan, the bishops, the priests, the deacons, and the blessed flock of twelve thousand, who were crowned for Christ’s sake; and on Saturday, the commemoration of the holy apostles, the fathers of the victorious martyrs. What bitter kinds of death did these unjust judges leave unused, without bringing them upon the martyrs, those mighty champions [?]? Or what severe tortures and fierce torments did the enemies of the church leave aside, without making Christ’s faithful servants endure them? Or what cups of suffering and bitterness did the enemies of our people neglect, without making those valiant ones, who fought with all their strength amid their afflictions, drink them? Some they tormented with hunger and thirst, and their bodies wasted away, and they died. Some were hung upside down in the midday heat; their flesh peeled away, and they died. Some, through the wrenching apart [?] of their shoulders as men stretched them, had their joints dislocated and died. Some they battered every day with foul blows, covering their sides [?] with bruises, and they died. Some had their ribs and bones broken with heavy clubs, and they died. Some they bound and threw out into the open and the frost until their bodies shriveled, and they died.

From some they horribly cut away the little flesh on their bones with shears, and they died. Some they painfully stripped of their skin by a harsh flaying, and they died. Some they savagely sawed through the vertebrae of their backs with saws, and they died. Some they violently bored through the ankles with drills, causing great suffering, and they died. For some, they arranged splinters of reed along their bodies and tightened ropes around them. They pulled them out one by one, along with flesh and sinews, and the victims died. Some they battered mercilessly with volleys of stones, and they died. Besides other tortures, they also cut off their noses and severed their ears and fingers. They blinded their eyes and broke their legs and knees with sledgehammers. Some they hung up by the heels of their feet. For some, they thrust potsherds beneath their armpits, and they died. For some, they filled sacks with ashes and thrust their heads into them. For some, they poured vinegar and [?] into their nostrils, and also smeared some of it on their wounds. For some, they mercilessly drove needles beneath their nails. For some, in the streets, [?] (not [?]?), they renewed their floggings day after day. And after all these
sufferings and fierce, cruel tortures, they cut off their heads with the sword.
The history of Karka of Beth Slok is finished, and of the holy martyrs who were crowned there and won victory through their noble martyrdom for our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
